newsitem.title: UK: UK's Prescott says bus regulation to be considered.
newsitem.headline: UK's Prescott says bus regulation to be considered.

text.p: Deputy prime minister John Prescott said on Thursday he will consider giving the rail regulator more powers and reviewing regulation for the bus industry.

Prescott, whose portfolio includes responsibility for both the environment and transport, is due to unveil the new Labour government's plans for environmental protection and for an integrated transport policy in a speech later on Thursday.
Prescott told a BBC interviewer he was considering a call from the rail franchising director, John O'Brien, to look into ways of beefing up his regulatory powers.

The deputy prime minister criticised the investment performance of Britain's rail infrastructure operator, Railtrack Plc, which on Thursday announced pretax profits of 346 million pounds, less than a year after it was privatised.

Prescott said the rail regulator had told him he was not convinced that Railtrack was meeting its programme for investment. "I am now looking at how I toughen up to get the investment to give railways the priority," he said.

Labour's Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown indicated before the May 1 election that Railtrack could be affected by the government's planned one-off windfall tax on the profits of privatised utilities. Prescott declined to give further details.
On the bus industry, which has also been a target for the former Conservative government's privatisation programme, Prescott said he would also consider whether new regulation was required.

Asked whether he was considering re-regulation for the bus industry as part of his transport strategy, Prescott said: "Yes, I think we are going to have to go thinking about the regulation of the buses.
"In fact privatisation has meant that at the peak time in some of our cities we get a great deal more buses running around less filled, more congestion, choking our cities.
"Now I think a better system is to go back to saying let us meet the needs of what people want and the needs of the environment," Prescott said.
